newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to tackle environmental rules breaches.
newsitem.headline: EU to tackle environmental rules breaches.

text.p: The European Commission is due to suggest ways on Tuesday to clean up EU countries' compliance with EU environmental laws intended to tackle problems such as air pollution and water and waste treatment.
Last year the Commission clocked 265 reported breaches of EU environmental law, a figure representing 20 percent of all the breaches notified to the executive.
The Commission is treading delicately with its planned paper, declining to say which countries are worst at transposing EU rules into national law and enforcing them.
"This is not a 'which is good, which is bad' exercise. There is a problem: too many cases are pending before the (European Court of Justice)," one Commission official said.
Commission figures for July 1996 showed that there were then 85 such cases pending before the European Court of Justice, which oversees questions of EU law.
Drafts of a 1995 compliance report for environmental laws, circulated in May, said Belgium was the worst offender for transposing EU law into national legislation.

Of the 133 EU directives applicable to Belgium at the end of last year, it had indicated compliance with only 111, or 83 percent. Not far behind was Italy, with 85 percent, Portugal and Finland, with 87 percent, and Greece, with 88 percent.

At the other end of the scale came the Netherlands and Denmark, who indicated compliance with 98 percent of applicable directives, ahead of France and Ireland on 95 percent with Sweden and Germany a further percentage point behind.

Breaches covered a whole slew of laws on waste, water and air pollution protection as well as ones governing habitat protection, access to information and impact assessments for the environmental damage caused during infrastructure projects.

The Commission's three-point plan is to include guidelines for countries to set up inspection systems where they do not already exist, an examination of national procedures for handling complaints and a look at how environmental groups and others can pursue legal actions against suspected law-breakers.
